title: Role-Based Authorization
description: Implement role-based authorization in ASP.NET Core and React applications for access control.

data.text: **Role-Based Authorization (RBAC)** is the most common approach to controlling access in applications. Instead of granting permissions to individual users, you assign users to **roles** and grant permissions to those roles. This makes managing access scalable and maintainable.

In a typical application, you might have thousands of users but only a handful of distinct access patterns. Without roles, you would need to configure permissions for each user individually - a maintenance nightmare. RBAC solves this by abstracting permissions into named roles.

data.title: Common Application Roles
items: **Admin**: Full system access, user management, configuration

data.text: ASP.NET Core Identity provides built-in role management. Roles are stored in the `AspNetRoles` table, and the many-to-many relationship between users and roles is maintained in `AspNetUserRoles`. The framework handles role creation, assignment, and validation automatically.

data.title: Configuring Role Services
Protecting Endpoints with Roles
Role Hierarchy is Not Automatic
data.text: ASP.NET Core Identity does not implement role hierarchy out of the box. A user in the 'Manager' role does NOT automatically inherit 'Editor' permissions. You must explicitly check for multiple roles or implement a custom role provider.

You can check roles programmatically inside controllers, services, or UI components. In ASP.NET Core, use `User.IsInRole("Admin")`. In React, you typically pass role information from the API in the JWT claims or a separate `/me` endpoint.

data.caption: Role-based authorization flow from login to endpoint access
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as ASP.NET Core
    participant DB as Database
    participant R as RoleManager
    U->>A: POST /login (credentials)
    A->>DB: Validate credentials
    DB-->>A: User found
    A->>R: GetRolesAsync(user)
    R-->>A: [Admin, Editor]
    A->>A: Generate JWT with role claims
    A-->>U: Return JWT
    U->>A: GET /api/admin/dashboard (JWT)
    A->>A: Validate token + roles
    alt User has required role
        A-->>U: 200 OK + data
    else Missing role
        A-->>U: 403 Forbidden
    end

data.title: Use Role Claims in JWT
data.text: When issuing JWTs, include the user's roles as claims. This avoids a database lookup on every request and enables stateless role validation in APIs.

data.title: RBAC Best Practices
items: Keep roles coarse-grained - fewer, well-defined roles are easier to manage
Never hardcode role names in multiple places - use constants or enums
Always validate roles server-side, never trust client-side role checks alone
Use role-based access for broad categories and combine with policies for specific actions
Document role responsibilities clearly for administrators and auditors

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: RBAC groups permissions into roles rather than assigning them per user
ASP.NET Core Identity provides built-in role management
Combine roles with policies for fine-grained control
data.takeaway: Role-Based Authorization is the foundation of access control. Master it before moving to more advanced patterns.
